# Exercise 1: Preprocessing and multivariate analysis

In this first exercise we are going to work with a real datasets
(*Palmer Penguins or the Penguin Data*) in order to put into practice
the concepts and techniques explained in the theory class about
preprocessing.

The work **must** be done in pairs.

```{r, warning=FALSE, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
list.of.packages = c(
```

The dataset will be simplified a bit.

```{r}
data("penguins")
?penguins

cols <- c("species", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", 
          "body_mass_g", "sex")
df <- penguins %>% 
  select(cols)

df_clean <- df %>% 
  select(-species) %>% 
  drop_na()

n <- nrow(df_clean) # Number of observations
p <- ncol(df_clean) # Number of variables
```

## Encoding

**Q1: Transform the *sex* variable so it can be used in the analysis.**

```{r}
# Use function as.numeric 
df_clean$sex <- as.numeric(df_clean$sex == "male") #logical vector where if "male" TRUE; 1 assigned
head(df_clean) #"male" is transformed to 1, "female" to 0
```

## Outliers analysis

Using the **df_clean** dataframe answer the following questions. Focus
on the variables *Flipper length* and *Bill length* for all the
analyses.

**Q2: Use the Local Outlier Factor method (with** $k=20$**) and identify
the top five outliers using the quantile** $97.5\%$ **to find the score
threshold. Generate a scatter plot to display the dataset, highlighting
any observations classified as outliers.**

```{r}
sum(is.na(df_clean)) #make sure no NAs

# Select study vars (flipper lenght, bill length)
df_lof <- df_clean[,c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]

# Compute LOF scores k = 20
lof_scores <-lof(df_lof, k=20) #set k to 20
#Set threshold
thr_lof <-quantile(lof_scores, 0.975, type = 7) #type 7 by default 

# Classify outliers according to threshold
df_lof$outlier_lof <-ifelse(lof_scores >= thr_lof, "Outlier", "Normal") 

# Identify Top 5 outliers
top5_idx_lof <-order(lof_scores, decreasing = TRUE) [1:5] #top 2.5% obs LOF score > 9.1 classified as outlier
df_lof$outlier_lof[top5_idx_lof] <- "Top 5 Outliers"

# Do scatter plot
ggplot(df_lof, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
          color = outlier_lof, shape = outlier_lof)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = outlier_lof), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal"         = 19,
                                "Outlier"        = 1,
                                "Top 5 Outliers" = 10)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal"         = "grey",
                                "Outlier"        = "blue",
              "Top 5 Outliers" = "blue")) +
  scale_size_manual(values  = c("Normal"         = 4,
              "Outlier"        = 4,
              "Top 5 Outliers" = 4)) +
  labs(title    = "Local Outlier Factor Detection",
       subtitle = paste("Threshold (97.5% quantile):", round(thr_lof, 2)),
       x        = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y        = "Bill Length (mm)",
    color    = "Classification",
    shape    = "Classification",
    size     = "Classification") +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Q3: Use the Isolation Tree algorithm with** $100$ **trees and identify
the top five outliers. Use the quantile** $97.5\%$ **to find the score
threshold Generate a scatter plot to display the dataset, highlighting
any observations classified as outliers.**

```{r}

# Select the study vars (flipper lenght, bill length)
df_iso <- df_clean[,c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]

# Train isolation forest 
iso_forest <-isolation.forest(df_iso, ndim=2, ntrees = 100) #set ntrees to 100

# Generate an anomaly score for each obs (between 0 and 1). The closer to 1, the more likely to be an outlier
iso_scores <-predict(iso_forest, df_iso, type = "score")

# Set threshold
thr_iso <-quantile(iso_scores, 0.975, type = 7) #type 7 by default 

# Classify outliers according to threshold
df_iso$outlier_iso <-ifelse(iso_scores >= thr_iso, "Outlier", "Normal") 

# Identify Top 5 outliers
top5_idx_iso <-order(iso_scores, decreasing = TRUE) [1:5] #top 2.5% obs are considered outliers
df_iso$outlier_iso[top5_idx_iso] <- "Top 5 Outliers" 

# Do scatter plot

ggplot(df_iso, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
          color = outlier_iso, shape = outlier_iso)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = outlier_iso), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Normal"         = 19,
                                "Outlier"        = 1,
                                "Top 5 Outliers" = 13)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Normal"         = "grey",
                                "Outlier"        = "red",
              "Top 5 Outliers" = "red")) +
  scale_size_manual(values  = c("Normal"         = 4,
              "Outlier"        = 4,
              "Top 5 Outliers" = 4)) +
  labs(title    = "Isolation Tree Outlier Detection (ntrees = 100)",
       subtitle = paste("Threshold (97.5% quantile):", round(thr_iso, 2)),
       x        = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y        = "Bill Length (mm)",
    color    = "Classification",
    shape    = "Classification",
    size     = "Classification") +
  theme_minimal()

```

**Q4: From the previous results, which observations can be considered
outliers? Why? Discuss what actions should be taken regarding them**

*"An outlier is an observation which deviates so much from the other
observations as to arouse suspicions that it was generated by a
different mechanism"* - Douglas Hawkins.

To conduct a more accurate comparison between algorithms, we will
visualize the "Top 5 outliers" detected by the Isolation Tree and the
Local Outlier Factor (LOF) methods. We can state that three in the top
five outliers detected, are coincidental in both.

```{r}

# Combine both methods into one dataframe
df_compare <- df_clean[, c("flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm")]
df_compare$lof_class <- df_lof$outlier_lof
df_compare$iso_class <- df_iso$outlier_iso

ggplot(df_compare, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey", size = 4, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = df_compare[df_compare$lof_class == "Top 5 Outliers", ],
             aes(color = "LOF"), size = 4, shape = 3) +
  geom_point(data = df_compare[df_compare$iso_class == "Top 5 Outliers", ],
             aes(color = "Isolation Forest"), size = 4, shape = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("LOF" = "blue", "Isolation Forest" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Top 5 Outliers: LOF vs Isolation Forest",
       x     = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y     = "Bill Length (mm)",
       color = "Method") +
  theme_minimal()
```

To determine the appropriate treatment for outliers, we should have more
information about the context of the study. Additionally, inspecting the
data values highlighted as outliers, might be useful, alongside the mean
bill and flipper lengths for these species may be beneficial.
Identifying an extreme outlier could indicate an error in data
collection or sampling.

## Missing values analysis

Now using the `df` dataframe, answer the following questions:

**Q5: Are there missing values? How we classify them (MCAR; MAR; MNAR)?
Quantify the quality of the data using the missing values.**

There are 19 missing values in the dataset distributed across variables:
"bill_depth_mm" (2), "bill_length_mm" (2), "flipper_length_mm" (2),
"body_mass_g" (2) and "sex" (11). Given a total number of 3096
observations, the missingness represents only 0,55% of the values,
consequently, the dataset is considered to be of high quality.

According to literature, we can classify missing values in three
different groups, thus being:

-   MCAR (Missing completely at random): when the missingness is purely
    a matter of chance.

-   MAR (Missing at Random): the missingness is related to observed data
    but not the missing values themselves.

-   MNAR (Missing Not at Random): the missingness depends on the
    unobserved value itself or other unmeasured factors.

```{r, warning=FALSE}

## Sum number of NAs in df
cat('Total number of NAs:', sum(is.na(df)), '\n')
(NAs_per_column = data.frame(NAs=colSums(is.na(df))))


## Quality of the data 
#Visualization
vis_miss(df, sort_miss = TRUE) #ggplot of the missingness inside the df
gg_miss_upset(df) #possible intersections bt the variables' missingnes
#Math
(19/(344*9))*100 #% of missing data overall; less than 1%
(11/344)*100 #% of missing in "sex"
(8/(344*4))*100 #% of NAs across num vars

## Classification between MCAR; MAR; MNAR
#MCAR test 
mcar_test(df) #check if the data is in the MCAR category (null hypothesis) p-value = 0.55 > 0.05, we fail to reject H₀ — meaning the data is consistent with MCAR

```

To categorize the missing data, we conduct an MCAR test with a level of
($\alpha = 0.05$). Since the resulting p-value is 0,55 we fail to reject
the null hypothesis and conclude that the numerical variables are
Missing Completely at Random (MCAR).

This means that the missingness is stochastic and unrelated to any other
observed variables. Consequently, the NAs we are dealing with can be
safely removed or imputed without introducing systematic bias into the
model.

**Q6: Perform a k-NN Imputation and a MICE imputation. Compare them.
Which imputation has better quality? Why?**

*Hint*: I provide code for the plots. Store the k-NN imputation in a
dataframe with name `df_1nn` and the MICE imputation in a dataframe with
name `df_mice` in order to perform the plots. Think carefully your
answers and check the consistency of the imputations.

```{r}

## k-NN and MICE imputations
df_1nn <- kNN(df, k = 1, imp_var=FALSE)
imp_mice <- mice(df, m = 5, printFla=FALSE) #number of default imputations
df_mice <-complete(imp_mice)

## Code provided for the plots
plot_columns <- cols[-c(1,6)]

for (column in plot_columns){
  comparison_df <- data.frame(
  KNN_1    = df_1nn[[column]],
  MICE     = df_mice[[column]]
  )
  plot_data <- comparison_df %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Method", values_to = "Value")
  
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Value, color = Method, fill = Method)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.1, linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
      title = "Comparison of Imputation Methods: 
      Distribution of flipper_length_mm",
      x = "Value of flipper_length_mm",
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1")
  
  print(p)
  
}
```

```{r}
subset_knn <- df_1nn %>%
  select(body_mass_g, sex) %>%
  mutate(Method = "kNN")

subset_mice <- df_mice %>%
  select(body_mass_g, sex) %>%
  mutate(Method = "MICE")

df_comparison <- bind_rows(subset_knn, subset_mice)

df_comparison <- df_comparison %>%
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, labels = c("Female", "Male")))

ggplot(df_comparison, aes(x = sex, y = body_mass_g, fill = Method)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Method) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of Body Mass by Sex across Imputation Methods",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

Once the computations are performed, it's difficult to observe any
differences between the results of both imputation methods, as they are
almost identical at first sight. Density plots reveal similar shapes,
and boxplot show very similar medians and IQRs.

To determine which method produces better results, we must consider
their characteristics and properties, according to the methodologies
used for computation. Thus being:

-   1-NN: it only uses values that actually exist in our data so the
    generating mechanism produces them. It is sensitive to outliers.

-   MICE: it preserves the distribution (mean and variance). It accounts
    for statistical uncertainty, therefore and shows better performance
    than 1-NN when working with datasets with higher rates of
    missingness.

Nonetheless, if we had to choose one method over the other, we would
stick with k-NN because the data we are working with has low missingness
and low dimensionality. Also, k-NN can handle local groupings (keep in
mind we are working with different types of penguin species).

MICE would outperform k-NN if we were working with a much higher
missingness ratio and a high-dimensional dataset. However, it is more
computationally costly.

Both 1nn and MICE imputation approaches converge to the same outliers,

## Multivariate matrices

Using the data without missing values (complete cases: `df_clean`)
answer the following questions:

**Q8: Compute the sample mean vector** $m$**, the centering matrix** $H$
**and the centered data matrix** $X_c$**. Only matrix and vector
operations are allowed.**

The sample mean vector $m$ is defined as:

$\mathbf{m}_{p \times 1} = \frac{1}{n} \left( \mathbf{1}^T X \right)^T$

The centering matrix $H$ is defined as:

$H = I - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T$

To obtain the centered data matrix $X_c$ we must operate:

$X_c = X - \mathbf{1}_{n \times 1} m^T = X - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T X = \left( I - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{1}^T \right) X$

Which can be synthesized as: $X_c = H X$

```{r}
##Previous steps

# Create matrix X
X <-as.matrix(df_clean[, sapply(df_clean, is.numeric)])

# Define terms
nX <- nrow(X) #number of obs
pX <- ncol(X) #number of vars
one_n <- matrix(1, nX, 1) #for easier calculations: create vector 1 with n dimensions
I_n <- diag(nX) #for easier computations

## Computation of the sample mean vector m (px1)
m <- (1 / nX) * t(one_n) %*% X

## Computation of the centering matrix H
H <- I_n - (1 / nX) * one_n %*% t(one_n)

## Computation centered data matrix Xc
X_c <- H %*% X

round(apply(X_c, 2, mean), 2)
```

**Q9: Using the centered** **data matrix compute the sample covariance
matrix** $S$**. Only matrix and vector operations are allowed.**

The sample covariance matrix $S$ is defined as:
$S = \frac{1}{n-1} X_c^T X_c$

```{r}
## Computation of sample covariance matrix S
(S <- (1 / (nX - 1)) * t(X_c) %*% X_c)
```

**Q10: Obtain the standardized data** **matrix** $X_s$ **and use it to
compute the sample correlation matrix** $R$**. Only matrix and vector
operations are allowed.**

The standardized data matrix is defined as follows:

$X_s = X_c D_s^{-1}$

where $D_s$ is expressed as: ${diag}(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_p)$; and where
$X_s$ can also be expressed as $X_s = H X D_s^{-1}$

The sample correlation matrix $R$ is defined as:

$R = D_s^{-1} S D_s^{-1} = \frac{1}{n-1} X_s^T X_s$

```{r, warning=FALSE}
## Previous calculations
#std_devs <- apply(X_c, 2, sd) #sd for each var
D_s <- diag(diag(sqrt(S))) #creation diag matrix Ds

## Computation of the standardized data matrix Xs
X_s <- X_c %*% solve(D_s) 

round(apply(X_s, 2, sd), 2)

## Computation of the sample correlation matrix R
#R <- solve(D_s) %*% S %*% solve(D_s)
(R = 1/(nX-1) * t(X_s) %*% X_s)
```
